title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, rendering the preregistered H1 (≥50% relative reduction) untestable as a confirmatory large‑effect hypothesis. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent to device configuration is a core NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize intent→configuration artifacts, but probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, and unsafe commands. Recent literature recommends hybrid designs that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops as operational floor‑safety nets. Rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics remain limited. We executed a narrowly scoped paired preregistered experiment to answer: Can a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot generation + frozen deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair—reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived artifacts; (ii) confirmatory statistics computed from those artifacts; (iii) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed contingency counts; and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory studies.
sections.related_work: Recent system demonstrations show intent→configuration synthesis using LLMs in lab settings but also report failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that affect safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) demonstrate that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors, motivating similar guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification tools (e.g., Minesweeper/Batfish, header‑space techniques) provide algorithmic foundations for static validators that check reachability and policy constraints without live changes [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Survey and standards work emphasize verification, provenance, and governance as open needs for operational adoption [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment sits at the intersection of these strands by measuring first‑pass validity under a validator+repair floor‑guardrail in a preregistered paired design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered study cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration documented the planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 used in power calculations; this assumption is central to later interpretation because the observed baseline diverged substantially.

Design and sampling: Paired within‑task design with a deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single LLM candidate per task served as the baseline response and as the starting point for guarded validation and possible repair. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing models operative remediation of one proposed plan but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces expected discordant pairs relative to independent‑draws designs (see Discussion).

Model and sampling determinism: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null. Because temperature was unset in the model configuration file, sampling determinism is unspecified (provider default sampling behavior applies); we therefore treat sampling determinism as unknown in inference and explicitly report this as a construct limitation (see Disclosure and Limitations). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 301 and repair_stage invocations = 1.

Validator and scoring semantics: A frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from task workflow policies. Scoring rule: full intent‑constraint validation—success only if normalized_configuration meets the task's required_sequence, expected_final_state, and workflow policies. Validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these structured traces determined repair invocation.

Repair adapter: The preregistered repair adapter is invoked only when the validator reports violations on the shared candidate and is restricted to a single repair attempt. The adapter receives the shared candidate and structured violation codes and attempts minimal edits to remove reported violations. Post‑repair validation used the same deterministic validator.

Contamination and exclusions: Preregistered contamination detection used deterministic normalized‑AST equality and near‑duplicate lexical thresholds; exact duplicates would be deterministically excluded and replaced from a reserved set. The primary analysis used the decontaminated paired set; any exclusions and replacements are archived in the execution manifest.

Primary estimand and analysis: Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Preregistered primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired binary outcomes, plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary analyses included binomial CIs for repair success conditional on initial failure and stratified checks by task difficulty. All numerical counts reported below are taken from archived analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair). No provider failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no contamination exclusions were applied.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency (archived paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair corresponds to pair-000229 (archived raw_results.jsonl entry for pair-000229 shows baseline score=0, guarded score=1 and two model calls for the guarded episode).

Inferential results (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00 on the observed contingency. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). These numbers reproduce exactly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Why H1 is not confirmably testable here: The preregistered H1 target (≥50% relative reduction) relied on the planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40. The observed baseline (299/300) leaves essentially no statistical headroom to detect the preregistered large relative effect: absolute paired difference equals (n10 − n01)/N, so with N=300 a single discordant pair yields a maximum resolvable absolute improvement of 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Consequently the preregistered large‑effect confirmatory hypothesis cannot be meaningfully evaluated on these data; our reported McNemar p and bootstrap CI are descriptive of the observed contingency and are presented without asserting that H1 is confirmed. This limitation is preregistered‑relevant and is reported here explicitly in Results per the peer‑review required revision.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) deterministically constrains inference: the paired difference equals 1/300 and the exact McNemar test conditions on the discordant total (here 1), which explains p = 1.00. The paired bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) conveys the same constrained uncertainty in interval form. These numerical facts are direct readings from archived artifacts and motivate our practical recommendations.

Design lessons and recommendations: (1) When planning confirmatory generate→verify→repair experiments, explicitly align preregistered effect targets with plausible baseline prevalences and the chosen pairing semantics (shared candidate vs independent draws). For N=300, an absolute improvement of ≈0.30 requires ≈90 net discordant pairs; planners should either calibrate task difficulty or use adversarial augmentation to achieve the expected number of initial failures. (2) If remediation of a single proposed plan is the operational question, prefer shared_initial_candidate pairing for ecological validity but account for reduced expected discordance in power computations. (3) If runtime semantics matter, integrate emulation/simulation stages and preregister how emulator outcomes map to success/failure rather than relying solely on static checks.

Diagnostics enabled by deterministic traces: The validator produced structured per‑task traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) that identify failure modes (syntax, missing commands, dependency violations). The single corrected episode (pair-000229) is traceable in raw_results.jsonl and repair traces archived for inspection. These traces are essential for explainability and reproducible post‑mortems.

Threats to validity: Internal validity—shared_candidate pairing increased within‑pair correlation and reduced discordant counts; this is preregistered. Construct validity—the validator used static checks rather than dynamic emulation, so runtime control‑plane or dataplane effects remain unmeasured. External validity—synthetic task bank and constrained vendor templates limit generalization. Conclusion validity—the paucity of discordant pairs (one) yields high sampling uncertainty for large preregistered effects; this is quantified in the archived bootstrap and exact test artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment evaluating a minimal guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini generation + frozen deterministic validator + ≤1 repair) on 300 paired tasks. Results: baseline 299/300 valid, guarded 300/300 valid; the single repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. The preregistered H1 target (≥50% relative reduction) depended on an assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40 and is not testable given the observed near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) and a single discordant pair. We therefore present artifact‑grounded descriptive inference (contingency counts, McNemar p = 1.00, paired bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.01]) and offer concrete, artifact‑traceable recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps studies: calibrate task difficulty/adversarially augment tasks to ensure sufficient initial failures or discordant counts, preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and add emulation when runtime semantics are material. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction—therefore H1 is not confirmably testable on these data.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Model sampling determinism was unspecified in the model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null); provider default sampling behavior applies and this unknown determinism constrains interpretation of generation variability.

Validation used deterministic static configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
